historical_timeline.summary: Born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland; the year is uncertain.
Struck in the head by an iron weight thrown by an overseer.
Headaches and sudden sleep spells with visions begin and persist through life.
Married Nelson Davis in Auburn, New York.
Reported surgery in Boston for headaches.
Died of pneumonia in Auburn, New York.
Temporal lobe epilepsy and post-traumatic narcolepsy proposed as explanations for the spells.

claims.statement: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in early 1822 by the National Park Service account, and was named Araminta, or Minty, by her parents, Ben and Rit Ross; she was the fifth of nine children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No birth record survives; the year is an estimate.

claims.statement: Her birth year is uncertain: the Dictionary of Canadian Biography gives 1820 or 1821, while the National Park Service and the Maryland State Archives give about 1822.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The case uses 1822 and records the alternative.

claims.statement: Hired out from the age of six, Tubman was struck in the head in her early teens, about age 13 in the mid-1830s, by an iron weight an overseer threw at another enslaved person at a village store; she was nearly killed, received little or no medical care, and was affected by the injury for the rest of her life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented injury that anchors the synthetic episode. The Maryland State Archives states that the blow broke her skull.

claims.statement: After the injury Tubman had headaches and sudden spells of sleep that came on even in the middle of work or conversation, at frequent intervals, and ended abruptly after a few minutes, along with vivid dreams and visions; contemporaries described the spells into her old age.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Lay descriptions; the modern label is uncertain.

source_links.locator: Seizures and bouts of somnolence for the rest of her life

claims.statement: Historians have proposed that the injury caused temporal lobe epilepsy, citing dreamlike trances in which she appeared conscious.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective proposal; it stays off the active problem list.

claims.statement: A 2023 review argued that temporal lobe epilepsy is unlikely, because she could be roused and no auras, automatisms, or post-ictal confusion were described, and proposed post-traumatic narcolepsy instead, while concluding that no definitive explanation is possible.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A second retrospective proposal; it is linked to, not confirmed by, the synthetic diagnosis.

claims.statement: In her later years Tubman said that a Boston surgeon had opened her skull to relieve her headaches; historians place the operation in the late 1890s at Massachusetts General Hospital, but no record of it has been found.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own account, published by her biographer Sarah Bradford in 1901; the date and procedure are unconfirmed.

claims.statement: Tubman married John Tubman in 1844, escaped to Philadelphia in 1849, guided about 70 people to freedom by 1860, served the Union army in South Carolina as a nurse, scout, and spy, and settled in Auburn, New York, where she married Nelson Davis in 1869.
Tubman died of pneumonia in Auburn, New York, on March 10, 1913.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate lifelong episodic spells and chronic headache after an adolescent traumatic brain injury in an older adult: use EEG, brain MRI, ambulatory EEG, polysomnography, and a multiple sleep latency test to tell sleep attacks from focal seizures, recognize and withdraw medication overuse, choose non-sedating headache prevention and a wake-promoting agent, and keep both retrospective diagnoses, temporal lobe epilepsy and post-traumatic narcolepsy, graded as interpretation.

encounters.display: Same-day sick visit for vomiting and diarrhea

documentation.chief_complaint: Vomiting and watery diarrhea for two days

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Tubman is a 75-year-old woman with chronic post-traumatic headache on candesartan 16 mg for prevention and provisional narcolepsy without cataplexy on modafinil 100 mg each morning, who asked for a same-day visit. Two days ago, a day after a community supper at which several other guests later became ill, she developed sudden nausea and vomited four times, followed by watery diarrhea six to eight times a day. The vomiting stopped yesterday; the diarrhea is easing, with three loose stools since midnight. There has been no blood or black stool. Her highest temperature at home was 37.8 °C. She has kept down small sips of water and broth since yesterday afternoon but little food. Her urine has been dark and less frequent, and she has felt light-headed when she stands up, without fainting or falling. She took candesartan and modafinil yesterday and this morning. A dull headache came with the illness; she took acetaminophen on both days and no ibuprofen, keeping to her headache plan. She has had two unplanned sleep episodes in the past two days, both while seated, compared with her recent rare episodes.

assessment_plan.display: Acute viral gastroenteritis, likely norovirus, with mild dehydration
assessment_plan.assessment: Acute watery, non-bloody diarrhea after a common-source exposure, already improving, with low-grade temperature only. Mild volume depletion: orthostatic change, dry mouth, and a creatinine of 1.21 mg/dL (eGFR 47), up from 0.88 in August, a prerenal rise while taking an angiotensin receptor blocker. Stool testing and antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated watery diarrhea of less than a week
plan: Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts, aiming for pale urine; then a normal diet as tolerated
Loperamide may be used for comfort if there is no fever above 38 °C and no blood in the stool

Hand washing with soap and water, which works better than alcohol gel against norovirus; clean bathroom surfaces with a bleach solution; do not prepare food for others until 48 hours after symptoms end
Rise slowly, sit to wash, and have someone nearby when she showers until the light-headedness is gone
Return or call the same day for blood in the stool, temperature above 38.5 °C, no urine for 12 hours, inability to keep fluids down, fainting, or a fall

assessment_plan.assessment: Headache with dehydration on two days, managed within her limit of acute medicine on no more than 2 days a week. Candesartan with volume depletion raises the risk of kidney injury
plan: Hold candesartan until she has been eating and drinking normally for a full day, then restart 16 mg daily

Acetaminophen as needed, no more than 3 g a day and within her 2-days-a-week limit; no ibuprofen or other NSAIDs, which can harm the kidneys during dehydration and risk a return of medication-overuse headache
Repeat the basic metabolic panel one to two weeks after restarting candesartan, at the wellness visit

assessment_plan.assessment: More unplanned sleep episodes during an acute illness, as expected with poor sleep and dehydration
plan: Continue modafinil 100 mg each morning once she is keeping fluids down
Keep the two scheduled naps and add rest as needed; sit down for tasks while she is unwell

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Tubman returns for her subsequent annual wellness visit, two weeks after a sick visit for viral gastroenteritis. She completed the health risk assessment before the visit. The illness resolved within four days; she restarted candesartan once she was eating and drinking normally, and the light-headedness has gone. Since her last wellness visit she has had no falls, emergency visits, or hospital stays. She takes candesartan and modafinil every day, uses acetaminophen about once a week, and has taken no ibuprofen since the spring. Her headache diary shows headache days holding near the August level. With modafinil and two scheduled naps, unplanned sleep episodes are again rare and happen only while she is seated. She does not drive. She runs a busy household and is active in her church. Her one concern is safety at home if a sleep episode comes on while she is cooking or bathing.
